subject: Anthropology
title: Artifacts and Ecofacts
description: A short lesson to help you apply Artifacts and Ecofacts.

hook.text: A clay pot is an artifact — someone made it. A charred seed is an ecofact — nature made it, humans used it.

buildup.text: Artifacts are objects made or modified by humans: tools, pottery, weapons, jewelry, and buildings.

discovery.text: Ecofacts are natural objects found in human contexts: animal bones, seeds, pollen, and soil samples.

twist.text: Ecofacts often reveal more about daily life than artifacts. What people ate tells you how they actually lived.

climax.text: Together, artifacts and ecofacts paint a full picture — what people made and what nature provided to sustain them.

punchline.text: Objects and nature together tell the human story.

quiz.question: What is an ecofact?
options: A natural item found in a human context

details.summary: Artifacts are objects made or modified by humans — tools, pottery, jewelry. Ecofacts are natural materials found in archaeological context — animal bones, seeds, pollen — that reveal human interaction with the environment. Together they reconstruct past lifeways.
details.whyItMatters: The artifact-ecofact distinction reminds archaeologists to study not just human creations but the environments humans inhabited. Ecofacts often reveal more about daily life — diet, climate, agriculture — than the most spectacular artifacts.
takeaways: Artifacts are human-made objects; ecofacts are natural materials in context
Ecofacts reveal diet, environment, climate, and agricultural practices
Both categories are essential for reconstructing past lifeways

faq.question: What can ecofacts tell us that artifacts cannot?
faq.answer: Animal bones reveal diet and hunting patterns. Pollen shows what plants grew nearby. Charred seeds indicate crops cultivated. Soil chemistry reveals land use. Ecofacts reconstruct the environment and subsistence practices that shaped daily life.

faq.question: Are features different from artifacts and ecofacts?
faq.answer: Yes. Features are non-portable evidence of human activity — hearths, postholes, walls, storage pits. They cannot be removed from the site and must be studied in place. Features reveal how spaces were organized and used.
